t: #3596 Minimum Cost Path with Alternating Directions I — Parity Argument
o: Odd moves must go right/down (positive), even moves must go left/up (negative). If the path has T moves, it contains o = ⌈T/2⌉ positive unit-steps and e = ⌊T/2⌋ negative ones, so the sum of the net displacements over both axes equals o − e ∈ {0, 1}. Reaching (m−1, n−1) requires net displacement (m−1) + (n−1) = m+n−2 in total, hence m+n−2 ≤ 1. That leaves only three solvable grids: 1×1 (stay put, cost 1), and 1×2 / 2×1 (single move, cost 1 + 2 = 3). Everything else returns −1. Examples confirm: (1,1)→1, (2,1)→3.
k: Positive steps only occur on odd moves and negative on even moves, so total net displacement ≤ 1.
Required total displacement is m+n−2, so only m+n−2 ≤ 1 grids are reachable.
Closed-form answers: 1 for 1×1, 3 for 1×2 or 2×1, otherwise −1.

a.i: Count odd/even moves and compare with the required Manhattan displacement. Since each odd move contributes +1 and each even move −1 across the two axes combined, o − e must equal m+n−2, which forces the three tiny cases above.
s: Else if (m,n) is (1,2) or (2,1) return 3 (entry 1 + entry 2).

a.n: Approach 2: BFS over (cell, move parity) — sanity checker
a.i: A direct simulation confirms the analysis: BFS on states (row, col, parity of next move number), expanding right/down on odd moves and left/up on even ones. It terminates quickly because the state space is finite and dead ends prune naturally; it is also a great way to verify the formula on small grids during a contest.
s: Start from (0,0) with cost 1 and next-move number 1.
Expand the two legal directions for the current parity, paying entry cost of the new cell.
Mark visited (cell, next parity) to avoid loops.
Return the cost when the destination is entered; −1 if the queue empties.
a.t: Exponential-ish exploration in the worst theoretical case but instant on solvable inputs; intended as verification, not the 10^6-scale submission

w: Always present the parity proof — with m, n up to 10^6, simulation cannot be the submitted solution. Pitfall: assuming longer wandering paths can help; they cannot, because negative-direction moves cancel positive ones one-for-one. Follow-up: Part II of this problem adds wait costs, which changes the analysis completely (see next problem).
